messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 52
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Maid
- Trauma Type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
- Pcl5: 51

# The Weight of a Moment

Rajan is a fifty-two-year-old South Asian man who works as a hotel housekeeper, pushing his cart through the long corridors of a downtown high-rise hotel with the quiet efficiency that comes from nearly two decades in the trade. He is methodical by nature — a man who folds towels with precision and notices when a chair has been moved an inch out of place. It is this same attentiveness, his supervisors have always said, that makes him exceptional at his work. Which is why what happened three years ago continues to devastate him in ways he cannot fully articulate, even to himself.

It was an ordinary Tuesday morning. Rajan was mopping the marble floor of the hotel lobby after a guest had tracked in rainwater near the entrance. He had placed the yellow warning signs, the way he always did, the way he had done hundreds of times before. But the signs were angled slightly wrong, or perhaps the light caught them poorly, or perhaps the elderly woman simply did not see them. She came around the corner quickly, her heel struck the wet marble, and she went down hard. Rajan heard the crack before he saw her fall. She fractured her hip and her wrist. She was eighty-one years old. She spent months in rehabilitation and never fully recovered her previous mobility.

In the immediate aftermath, Rajan knelt beside her on that wet floor, holding her hand and calling for help, watching her face contort in pain. He replays this image constantly — her expression, the angle of her wrist, the sound. He was cleared of any formal negligence. The hotel's insurance handled everything. His supervisors told him it was an accident. None of that has mattered.

In the months that followed, Rajan stopped sleeping well. He would lie in the darkness of his small apartment — he has lived alone since his divorce seven years ago, and his two adult children are settled in another city — and the sound of her fall would arrive without warning, as vivid and percussive as the moment itself. He began waking at two or three in the morning, heart hammering, unable to return to sleep. During the day, he moves through his shifts with a hypervigilance that exhausts him. He checks and rechecks the placement of every warning sign. He mops more slowly than he used to, stopping repeatedly to test the floor with his own foot. His colleagues have noticed that he flinches whenever someone walks quickly around a corner.

He avoids the lobby entirely when he can arrange it. He has requested reassignment to the upper floors and has never explained why. When he cannot avoid the lobby, he feels a tightness in his chest that begins before he even steps off the elevator — a dread that tightens around him like a fist. He has had several moments at work where he has had to step into a supply closet simply to breathe.

Rajan carries a particular kind of guilt that he describes, when he speaks of it at all, as feeling like a stone in his chest that never moves. He does not believe he is a careless man, and yet he cannot reconcile that belief with what his hands and his mop and his slightly misplaced signs did to another person's body and life. He has looked up the woman's name online more than once, searching for any information about her, though he does not know what he hopes to find or what he would do with it.

He has become withdrawn in ways that worry even him. He rarely speaks to neighbors. He declined an invitation to his daughter's home last Diwali, telling her he was unwell, which was not entirely untrue. He sits most evenings with the television on but does not watch it. He describes himself as feeling "far away from everything," as though the world is continuing at a normal pace just beyond a pane of glass he cannot break through.

He came to therapy only because his physician, noting his sleep disturbance and weight loss, insisted. He sat in the first session with his hands folded tightly in his lap and said, simply, "I hurt someone. I need to understand why I cannot move past it."
